extracted.intended_audience: businesses (especially UK companies) planning to trade or operate in Vietnam
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and standards for protecting, registering and enforcing various forms of intellectual property (patents, designs, trade marks, copyright, etc.) when doing business in Vietnam, including preventative measures and enforcement routes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Register IP rights to enjoy protection
rubrics_metrics.description: To enjoy most types of intellectual property (IP) rights in Vietnam, you should register them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents (inventions, utility models, industrial designs) require individual registrations in Vietnam; for some rights you can use international routes (PCT for patents; Madrid Protocol for trade marks). Copyright requires no registration but registering with the National Copyright Office is advisable. 'Priority rights' under the Paris Convention can make earlier filings effective in Vietnam if filed within time limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent system: invention patents vs utility solution patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Vietnam distinguishes between patents (invention patents) and utility solution patents (utility models/minor patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules for utility solution patents are similar to invention patents but a utility solution is not required to demonstrate an 'inventive step'. Invention patents protect for a maximum of 20 years; utility solution patents are valid for ten years. Vietnam operates under the 'first to file' principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial design protection duration and renewals
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial designs are protected for a maximum of five years, renewable for two consecutive periods of five years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Register industrial designs with NOIP. The document notes the design term structure (5 + 5 + 5) as the statutory maximum protection period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade mark scope, registration term and process
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade marks protect signs, colours and other visual devices (including three-dimensional objects) used to identify products/services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration takes up to 15 months (13 months in theory). A trade mark is valid for ten years and may be renewed indefinitely for further ten-year periods. Trade marks can be registered in Vietnam or via the Madrid Protocol for multi-jurisdiction coverage. Trade names may acquire rights through use rather than formal registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain name allocation and cybersquatting risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Domain names are allocated on a first come, first served basis so must be registered to avoid 'cybersquatting' by abusers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Register relevant domain names promptly to prevent third parties from acquiring them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customs recordal and Customs enforcement powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Vietnamese Customs have powers to monitor counterfeit or pirated goods and may act against both imports and exports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formal customs recordal system allows IP rights owners to register their marks with Customs; Customs can assist in border enforcement against infringing goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three enforcement routes: administrative, civil and criminal
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three levels at which rights may be enforced in Vietnam: administrative action, civil court action and criminal prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative action: majority route, generally fast and comparatively straightforward; sanctions include warnings, fines, seizure or destruction of counterfeit goods, business licence suspension and re-exportation of infringed imported/transit goods. Civil court action: rare due to judicial training and lack of specialist courts, but preliminary injunctions and compensation are available. Criminal prosecution: authorities or rights owners may apply; penalties can include fines, imprisonment and in serious cases the death penalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative enforcement is common but limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative action is the usual route for dealing with infringements, offering low-cost, quick results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deterrent effect is limited because of low levels of penalties and lack of compensation. Administrative enforcement is complicated by the large number of bodies involved and agencies may struggle to keep up with legal changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-help measures to reduce copying and leakage
rubrics_metrics.description: There are various things you can do to make it harder for infringers to copy your product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: think about product design to reduce easy reproduction; include effective IP clauses in employment contracts and educate employees; ensure physical protection and secure destruction methods for documents, drawings, tooling, samples, machinery; avoid packaging 'leakages' that counterfeiters can use to pass off fakes; check production over-runs to ensure genuine product isn't sold under a different name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take preparation steps to avoid IP problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared and take preventive steps to anticipate potential IP issues in Vietnam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take advice from Vietnamese IP experts; consult publications and websites; carry out risk assessments and due diligence on organisations/individuals; take professional advice from lawyers, local diplomatic posts, Chambers of Commerce, business groups; talk to other businesses; consult agents/distributors on safeguarding rights; check with trade mark or patent attorneys for prior registrations; stick to familiar business methods rather than changing practices because you are in a different country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign responsibility for IP protection internally
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure everyone in your business takes some responsibility for IP protection; consider nominating a specific manager.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many businesses depend on IP as a valuable asset. Nominate a manager—ideally legally-trained if you have a legal department—to understand and protect IP rights across the business and with external partners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top practical tips for protecting IP in Vietnam
rubrics_metrics.description: Key practical recommendations summarised for businesses operating in Vietnam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stick to normal business instincts; prevention is better than cure; assess market risks and prepare; take self-help measures; make sure everyone in the business values IP; register your IP rights; create good relationships with organisations that can help; consider mediation before defensive action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright protections and duration (Berne Convention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vietnam is a Berne Convention signatory; copyright protection durations are set by that framework and local law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimum protections noted: 50 years from publication for cinematographic, photographic, dramatic, applied art and anonymous works; 50 years after the death of the author for other works. Computer programs are included within copyright legislation where 'computer programs as such' cannot be patented. Registration with the National Copyright Office is advisable.

rubrics_metrics.name: International treaty participation and filing options
rubrics_metrics.description: Vietnam is a party to various international IP agreements which affect filing strategies and rights recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vietnam is a WTO member and signatory to the Paris Convention (priority rights), Berne Convention, Madrid Protocol (trade marks central filing), Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) for patents. Vietnam is not a signatory to the Hague Agreement (designs). Use international systems where available but note some rights (e.g., certain industrial designs) may require national filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfair competition legal framework and complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Unfair competition relating to IP is governed mainly by Vietnam’s Competition Law of 2005, with some provisions in IP law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures for handling unfair competition relating to IP are complicated and largely untried—expect uncertainty and potential procedural complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration authorities and practical filing notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Different Vietnamese offices administer different IP areas and have specific roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NOIP (National Office of Intellectual Property) administers industrial property rights (patents, utility solutions, designs, trade marks). The Copyright Office of Vietnam handles copyright and related rights. For plant varieties there is a separate Plant Variety Protection Office. Use relevant offices and consider international routes (PCT, Madrid) where applicable.
